questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman was reviewed as part of contact tracing for an acute case of hepatitis A in a childcare center. She worked as a nursery nurse, had been born and brought up in the United States, and had no recent travel. She was asymptomatic. She was usually well and was not taking any regular medications.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Screen for underlying immunodeficiency or liver disorders

questions.explanation: Give single-dose HAV vaccination. Postexposure prophylaxis is warranted as the index case was in a childcare center, caring for children likely to still be in diapers. Food handlers and close household/sexual contacts of a confirmed case would also be advised to receive PEP . For healthy persons aged 12 months to 40 years, single-antigen hepatitis A vaccine at the age-appropriate dose is preferred to immunoglobulin because of the vaccine’s advantages, including long-term protection and ease of administration, as well as the equivalent efficacy of vaccine to immunoglobulin. Adults ≥40 or with immunocompromised or chronic liver disease also required HAV immunoglobulin. For more information, see https://www.cdc.gov/hepatit is/hav/havfaq.htm.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q22

questions.question: Man comes back from India with Hepatitis A.

parts.text: What PEP do you provide for his pregnant wife, 9 month old, 15 month old. He wants to go back to India, does he need hepatitis A vaccine? His sister has one dose 9 years ago. She wants to go to India too! she need 1 or 2 doses? Why?

questions.model_answer:
Household contacts should receive PEP as soon as possible (ideally <2 weeks post-exposure):
- Pregnant wife (healthy, 12mo–40yr equivalent adult): hepatitis A vaccine, 1 dose (inactivated vaccine is not contraindicated in pregnancy; IG can be added per risk assessment but is not mandatory in this age group).
- 9-month-old infant (<12 months): too young for vaccine — give immune globulin (IG) 0.1 mL/kg only.
- 15-month-old (12mo–40yr, healthy): hepatitis A vaccine, 1 dose.
Man himself: he already has acute hepatitis A and will develop natural immunity, so he does not need vaccine before returning to India.
Sister (1 dose 9 years ago, planning travel): needs only 1 further dose (i.e., dose 2 of the 2-dose series), not restart with 2 doses — there is no maximum interval between doses; the first dose primes long-lasting immune memory, so the series is simply completed with the second dose regardless of the delay.

parts.text: Name 6 people or groups of people to give pre-exposure prophylaxis for Hep A

questions.model_answer: Groups recommended pre-exposure prophylaxis (hepatitis A vaccine): (1) international travelers/workers to high- or intermediate-endemicity countries, (2) men who have sex with men, (3) people who use injection or noninjection drugs, (4) persons with chronic liver disease, (5) persons receiving clotting factor concentrates, (6) persons who work with HAV in research settings or with nonhuman primates. (Also acceptable: close contacts of international adoptees from endemic countries, people experiencing homelessness, anyone who wants immunity.)

parts.text: How do you diagnose
What prophylaxis for family members (mother, 5 y.o brother, 10 months old sister)

cohort_answer.text: How do you diagnose: Serum antibody (IgM). Prophylaxis for family members: Vaccination for all of them; And IVIG if any of them are immunocompromised

parts.text: Give 6 populations / patient groups who should have Hepatitis A vaccination as pre-exposure prophylaxis.

questions.model_answer: Groups recommended for Hepatitis A pre-exposure vaccination: (1) Travelers to hepatitis A-endemic regions. (2) Men who have sex with men. (3) Injection and non-injection illicit drug users. (4) Persons with chronic liver disease (including chronic hepatitis B or C). (5) Persons with clotting factor disorders receiving factor replacement therapy. (6) Individuals with occupational exposure risk (e.g., researchers handling HAV, primate handlers) or residents/staff of institutions for individuals with developmental disabilities.

questions.question: Scenarios involving PEP For HAV. Man comes back from trip in India with symptoms concerning for HAV.

parts.text: A) What is the single best test to confirm dx?
B) Assuming diagnosis confirmed, what do you do for each of the following individuals: Adult wife, 5 year old child, 9 month old child
C) The patient recovers, and is now planning a trip back to India 6 months later. He asks whether he still needs to be vaccinated. What do you tell him?

D) A woman who has received one dose of HAV vaccine 9 years ago is planning another trip and wants to know whether she should receive 1 or 2 doses of vaccine this time around. What do you tell her and why?
E) What are the dosage schedules for HAV?

cohort_answer.text:
Hepatitis A IgM (gold standard, + at 5-10 days, remains + for 3-12 months)
Adult wife - vaccinate within 14 days (if <60 years); 5 year old child - vaccinate within 14 days; 9 month old child - vaccinate within 14 days
Patients who acquire HAV (naturally or via vaccine) are immune for life, cannot get HAV twice. Advise Hep B vaccine if not already vaccinated
One dose of monovalent HA vaccine given for primary immunization with booster dose at least 6-36 months later for lifelong protection; she only needs one additional dose
2 doses: 0 and 6 months

questions.question:
Q9 (2010 PM, 2018)
Scenarios involving PEP for HAV.
Man comes back from trip in India with symptoms concerning for HAV. Multiple-part question.

parts.text: A. What is single best test to confirm diagnosis?
Assume the diagnosis is confirmed, what do you do for each of the following individuals who have potential exposure in the household? -Adult wife -5 year old child -9 month old child
C. The patient recovers, and is now planning trip back to India six months later. He asks whether he still needs vaccine. What do you tell him?

D. A woman who has received one dose of HAV vaccine nine years ago is planning another trip and wants to know whether she should receive one or two doses of vaccine this time around. What do you tell her and why?
E. What are the dosage schedules for HAV?

cohort_answer.text: A) Hepatitis A IgM. B) Adult wife: vaccinate with 1 dose of hep A vaccine if no prior vaccination hx, second dose at 6 months, ideally within 14 days but ASAP preferred. 5 year old child: vaccinate. 9 month old child: vaccinate; immunoglobulin indicated in 0-12 month age group but vaccination preferred if >6 months. C) Natural infection confers lifelong immunity for HAV; no need for vaccine.

questions.question: Q49. A woman who has received one dose of HAV vaccine 9 years ago is planning another trip and wants to know whether she should receive one or two doses of vaccine this time around.

parts.text: What do you tell her and why? What are the dosage schedules for HAV?

cohort_answer.text: Only 1 additional dose of HAV vaccine needed. Usual dosing at 0 and 6-36 months.

questions.question: For the following organisms, list the latest time that Ig can be given as PEP.

parts.text: Measles
VZV
Hepatitis B
Hepatitis A
Rabies

cohort_answer.text: Measles: 6 days (vaccine within 72 hrs). VZV: 96 hours – 10 days. Hepatitis B: 12 hours, up to 7 days for needle and infants, 14 days for sexual contact. Hepatitis A: 14 days. Rabies: up to Day 7 after vaccine given.

questions.question: You see a patient with severe sepsis. He recently traveled to Florida where he consumed many raw oysters.

parts.text: What is the most likely bacteria causing his infection?
List THREE clinical syndromes associated with this bacteria.
List THREE risk factors for severe sepsis with this bacteria.
List TWO common viral infections that are associated with eating raw oysters.

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely bacteria: Vibrio vulnificus.
b) 3 clinical syndromes: (1) primary septicemia (often fulminant bacteremia), (2) wound infection/necrotizing skin and soft tissue infection (from seawater/shellfish exposure), (3) gastroenteritis.
c) 3 risk factors for severe sepsis: (1) chronic liver disease/cirrhosis, (2) iron overload states (e.g., hemochromatosis), (3) immunocompromising conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus, chronic renal disease, or immunosuppressive therapy).
d) 2 viral infections associated with raw oyster consumption: norovirus and hepatitis A virus.
